title: Science Through the Lens of Investing
text:
I recently returned from a conference in Berlin, Germany. For me, it was a very successful conference, and I achieved the goals I had set for myself. But after observing and talking with many colleagues, I also came away with some interesting thoughts about modern scientific research.
They reminded me, surprisingly, of investing.
I noticed that there were a few young researchers who were exceptionally good—arguably well ahead of their peers. But perhaps because they had gone so far, so quickly, some of their ideas were very new and difficult for both the panel and much of the audience to immediately grasp.
Judging from the reactions of the audience and some of the more senior researchers, their presentations did not seem to receive as much recognition as I might have expected.
Meanwhile, other colleagues—also very capable researchers—presented work that was somewhat more familiar. Some aspects might even have been slightly outdated, but the ideas were easier to understand and closer to what the audience already knew.
Their work received considerable recognition, and they were among those who really stood out at the conference.

title: Science Through the Lens of Investing
section: Science may work in a similar way
text:
Science may work in a similar way
I think something similar can happen in science.
The researchers receiving recognition today are undoubtedly talented. But there are also excellent researchers working on ideas that are newer, less familiar, or simply different from the mainstream.
Their work may eventually receive the recognition it deserves, but that can require time:

time to accumulate evidence,
time for ideas to mature,
and time for the wider field to catch up with a new way of thinking.

In investing, timing matters.
In research, communication and staying connected with your field matter too.
Perhaps having a good idea is only part of the challenge. Another part is communicating that idea in a way that allows other people to understand why it matters.

P.S. This reflection is entirely about colleagues who are more senior and experienced than I am—it is not about me. These are simply my personal observations and interpretations from the conference.
Have you noticed anything similar in your own field?
